children: By Koji Sobata and Shinji Abe / Yomiuri Shimbun Staff Writers

NEW YORK — Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi projected a united Japan-U.S. front together with U.S. President Donald Trump during talks Tuesday, aligning stances on China just two days ahead of Trump's meeting with his Chinese counterpart.

"Against the backdrop of an increasingly severe security environment ... I would like to seize this opportunity to demonstrate to the world how robust our alliance is through holding another round of meetings with Donald today here at this venue, the U.N. headquarters," Takaichi emphasized at the outset of the talks.

"So on this occasion I would like to cover a lot of agenda items. So why don't we ask the press corps to leave the room so that (we can start our) discussion," Takaichi said through an interpreter, prompting the media to exit.
Trump concurred, saying, "Well, you heard her," and refrained from taking questions from reporters, which typically take a long time.
United front
Takaichi had been determined to hold talks with Trump ahead of his planned summit meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday.
Her intention was to ensure that both nations present a united front on extensive issues, ranging from economic security, such as export curbs on critical minerals, to matters surrounding Taiwan.
With Beijing continuing its coercive actions in the East and South China Seas and other waters, Tokyo is deeply concerned over what agreement the unpredictable Trump might reach with Xi.
"(Depending on the content of any agreement,) Washington's security commitment to the Asia-Pacific region could erode," said a senior Japanese Foreign Ministry official.
After the U.S.-China summit in Beijing in May, it was revealed that Xi had singled out Takaichi for criticism.
Given the protracted strains in Japan-China relations, Japanese officials saw a need to make preparations in anticipation that Xi will push one-sided claims again at the upcoming summit.
U.S. motives
Takaichi's team explored opportunities to engage with Trump, including an informal standing chat, and ultimately arranged a 35-minute formal meeting.
"(The prime minister) said everything we wanted to say. She laid as much groundwork as possible ahead of the U.S.-China summit," a senior government official said.
"From Trump's attitude, you could really tell he cares about the prime minister and the bilateral relationship," said another person who attended the meeting.
The United States has seen ties with Canada and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization become strained over its tariff policies and military actions targeting Iran.

With the Trump administration becoming "increasingly isolated" internationally, as described by The Washington Post, the United States likely aimed to project strong ties with a major Indo-Pacific ally ahead of the U.S.-China summit.
Divide over ICC
Meanwhile, a clear divide between the two leaders came to the fore over the International Criminal Court, toward which Trump has expressed open hostility.
During the talks, the two leaders' discussion of the ICC remained on parallel tracks, according to a Japanese government source.
Trump slammed the ICC, a body that prosecutes war crimes, as an "evil group of people" during his speech Tuesday at the United Nations.
Amid mounting calls to hold Washington legally accountable for its military operations against Iran and other actions, Trump remains wary of facing prosecution by the ICC.
In Japan, strong backlash has spread over U.S. sanctions targeting ICC President Tomoko Akane.
Seeing discussions to be unavoidable in light of Japan's longstanding diplomatic posture of advocating the "rule of law," Takaichi brought up the issue during the meeting.
Takaichi also emphasized Japan's unwavering support for the ICC during her address Tuesday at the U.N. General Assembly.
Even so, anticipating pushback from Trump if she openly voiced concern over the U.S. sanctions, Takaichi measured her words carefully even in her address.
"It was a response handled on a fine line to ensure relations with Trump could be maintained," said a source close to the prime minister.
